headline: The Coventry Blitz
border_caption: A Union Flag hangs defiantly over the wreckage of central Coventry after the night-long Luftwaffe raid of November 14–15, 1940.

image.file: File:A Union Flag hangs defiantly from a building in the aftermath of the air raid which devastated the centre of Coventry on the night of 14-15 November 1940. H5598.jpg
image.note: A Union Flag hangs from a building in the centre of Coventry after the air raid of the night of November 14–15, 1940.

hook: November 14, 1940: for ten hours, 515 German bombers pounded the English city of Coventry. By morning, its medieval heart was gone.
body: The Luftwaffe code-named the raid Moonlight Sonata. Its targets were Coventry’s factories, which built aircraft engines, vehicles and munitions, but wave after wave of high explosives and incendiaries set the whole city center ablaze.

An estimated 568 people were killed, and more than 4,300 homes were destroyed. The medieval cathedral of St Michael burned to a shell. Coventry’s anti-aircraft guns fired more than 6,700 rounds that night and brought down just one bomber.

Joseph Goebbels began using a new word for wiping out a city: “coventriert,” or “Coventried.” Coventry chose a different legacy. Its ruined cathedral became a symbol of peace and reconciliation, and after the war the city twinned with Dresden.
